title: Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the K largest numbers. Explain why a min-heap of size K is the efficient structure and how it maintains the K largest seen so far.
shortTitle: Top K Numbers (Find the K Largest Numbers with a Min-Heap)
keyPoints: To find the K largest numbers, use a min-heap of size K where the root is the smallest of the K largest seen so far.
A new number replaces the root only if it is larger, keeping the heap always holding the K largest.
Time complexity is O(n log K), which is better than O(n log n) sorting when K is small relative to n.
Space complexity is O(K) for the heap.
Counter-intuitively, a min-heap finds the K largest and a max-heap finds the K smallest.
For streaming data, this approach processes each element once without needing the full array in memory.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K where a new number replaces the root only if it is larger, so the heap always holds the K largest numbers seen so far.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Min-heap of size K** – the root is the smallest of the K numbers currently kept, making the keep-or-discard decision a single O(1) peek.
- **Eviction rule** – a new number enters the heap only if it beats the root; it then replaces the root via poll-then-offer, which is O(log K).
- **Counter-intuitive choice** – to find the K largest you use a min-heap, not a max-heap, because the root being the smallest of the kept set is what lets you cheaply evict the weakest candidate.
- **Streaming friendly** – each element is processed once without needing the full array in memory.
- **O(n log K) time** – each of the n elements costs at most O(log K) for a heap operation.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day and the risk team wants the K biggest transactions for priority review. They keep a small bucket that holds only the K biggest so far, where the smallest of those K sits at the top for quick checking. Each new transaction only enters the bucket if it beats the smallest one currently in it, pushing that smallest one out.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem, and the counter-intuitive choice is that to find the K largest numbers you use a min-heap, not a max-heap. You keep the heap bounded to size K and seed it with the first K numbers. For every remaining number, you compare it against the heap root, which is the smallest of the K numbers you are currently keeping. If the new number is larger, you evict the root and insert the new number; if not, you discard it.

The reason the min-heap works is that the root is always the weakest candidate in your kept set, so deciding whether a new number deserves a place is a single constant-time peek, and eviction is one O(log K) heap operation. This gives O(n log K) time and O(K) space, which is far better than O(n log n) sorting when K is small relative to n.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to pull the K largest transaction amounts from a long daily stream for the risk team's priority review. He kept a size-K min-heap where each new amount only displaced the smallest kept amount if it was larger, processing millions of transactions without sorting them all.

The senior-level insight is understanding when to switch tools: quickselect gives O(n) average for a static array, sorting is simpler when K is close to n, and in distributed systems each node keeps its own top-K heap and results are merged at a coordinator.

Remember one sentence: min-heap of size K, evict the root only when a larger number arrives, and the heap always holds the K largest.
